source.title: Sparsity, Superposition, and Forgetting: A Mechanistic Study of Representation Retention in Continual Learning
source.authors: Jan Wasilewski; Jȩdrzej Kozal; Micha l Woźniak; Bartosz Krawczyk

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some equations and appendix table formatting are garbled, but the reported results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures feature-direction overlap in a controlled toy network, but uses its own continual-learning setup and measures rather than reproducing the original toy-model method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports qualitative outcomes for sparsity, superposition, retention, and effective rank. It also mentions task-wise accuracies as additional metrics, but no corresponding accuracy results are present in the supplied text. Architecture and sampling details are partly deferred to the appendix; do not infer results from cited works.
record.test_reason: The study measures directional overlap among ground-truth features as input sparsity varies in a bottlenecked toy encoder. This bears on V1's sparsity–superposition link, but in a new setting (sequential continual learning with replay, encoder width 5 or 9, 50 features) rather than the original toy-model recipe. The other results (retention, temporal dynamics, effective rank) concern forgetting and capacity allocation, not any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. It should also state the first takeaway: superposition rises over time with transient dips at task boundaries. In full: sparsity drives overlap; overlap harms retention mainly when representations are weak and fresh; sparser regimes give higher task effective rank.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a synthetic generator–separator pipeline, a bottlenecked encoder trained sequentially with experience replay, pure-feature probes, and effective-rank measurements. It does not reproduce the original toy-model training setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports qualitative robustness across alternative settings in Appendix Figures 7–10. It also says SINDy coefficient selection varies across runs while dominant interaction signs remain stable (Figures 11–12).

fits_no_version.finding: Superposition strength rises over training as tasks accumulate, dips transiently at task boundaries, then recovers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In continual learning, feature overlap grows with accumulated tasks and is transiently reduced at task boundaries.

fits_no_version.finding: Task-embedding effective rank increases with sparsity, with small contractions at task transitions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Tasks built from sparser features occupy higher-effective-rank latent regions.

fits_no_version.finding: SINDy fits locate the most negative retention in the low-strength, high-overlap regime; strong representations buffer overlap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overlap predicts representational forgetting mainly when feature representations are weak and recently introduced.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparser features tend to yield stronger representations (larger embedding norms).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In toy encoders, feature sparsity increases learned embedding norm.

record.problems: The evidence is from a controlled toy setup with uniform feature sparsity and disjoint task supports. The retention proxy is change in representation strength rather than classifier performance or standard continual-learning forgetting metrics. The supplied text reports qualitative results without numerical values or uncertainty estimates, and describes robustness figures without giving their underlying values.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant result rows left out.

untested.parts: Near-orthogonality of directions, a sparsity-dependent phase transition, and regular geometric configurations. Only the direction 'sparser features have more overlap' is reported.
Entire version: no neuron-level polysemanticity, no variation of feature importance, and no dedicated-dimension analysis.
Entire version: no LLMs or SAEs.
Entire version: features are assumed to be directions, not tested against multi-dimensional alternatives.

missing.what: Task-wise accuracy curves, said to be in the Appendix but absent from the supplied text.
Numeric S(i,t) values per sparsity level and any norm-normalised overlap (e.g. cosine) measure needed to separate overlap from representation strength.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T2 to T3 because the setting is continual learning rather than the original single-task toy model. The V2 label is dropped because no neuron-level or importance-based test is made. The sole V1 support is qualitative. S(i,t) uses unnormalised projections, so the reported overlap increase may partly reflect the larger norms the authors also report for sparser features. The paper's own pairing of rising overlap with rising effective rank is not reconciled.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not establish near-orthogonality, a sparsity-dependent transition point, or regular geometric configurations. It tests directional overlap as sparsity varies in its continual-learning toy setting.

The paper imposes a latent bottleneck and measures overlap and task effective rank, but does not test neuron-level polysemanticity or vary feature importance to determine whether important features get dedicated dimensions.
No alternative cause of polysemanticity is tested.
No LLMs, neuron-spread measurements, or sparse dictionary features are studied.
No SAE features or tests of their completeness, stability, or canonical status.
The paper defines learned features as directions or approximately linear subspaces, but does not compare one-dimensional with multidimensional features.

rows.operation_detail: Measured pure-feature directional superposition strength S(i,t) across feature-sparsity regimes.
rows.measure: Superposition strength S(i,t), an aggregate of projections of other feature embeddings onto the feature direction
rows.value: The text reports systematically larger S(i,t) for sparser features and says sparser signals are represented with more directional sharing.
rows.note: The text gives qualitative comparisons, not numerical S(i,t) values. The study describes a latent bottleneck but does not compare against a no-bottleneck control.
rows.check: Qualitative only: no S(i,t) values, baseline or uncertainty. S sums squared projections of unnormalised other-feature embeddings, so it rises when other features' norms rise. The paper also says sparser features get stronger representations, which confounds overlap with norm. The sparsity axis (0.15 vs 0.2) is not clearly oriented. Neuron-level polysemanticity and feature importance are not measured, so the V2 link is removed.

tranche.reason: Tests the sparsity–superposition relationship in a new setting: sequential continual learning with experience replay and a bottlenecked classifier encoder.

source_check.notes: Eq. (3) normalizes the target direction but not other feature embeddings, so larger embedding norms can increase S without greater angular overlap; the paper also reports stronger representations for sparser features. No no-bottleneck comparison is reported.

statements.correction: Sparsity–overlap results are qualitative, without numerical S values or quantified uncertainty. Section 5 reports coefficient-selection variability across runs and stable dominant interaction signs; Figures 11–12 concern SINDy instability.
statements.problem: The overlap finding and measurement caveat are accurate. The blanket claim of no reported uncertainty overlooks the reported SINDy coefficient variability and stability analyses.
